title: Data compression methods all compress repetition and nesting but little else

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Data compression methods all compress repetition and nesting but little else

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Structurally different lossless data compression methods (run-length, block/Huffman, pointer-based and two-dimensional schemes) have remarkably similar capabilities: they compress uniform regions, repetitive behavior and to some extent nested behavior, but achieve no substantial compression of more complex behavior even when it is generated by very short programs.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Essentially every method, for example, will successfully compress large regions of uniform color. And most methods manage to compress behavior that is repetitive, and at least to some extent behavior that is nested—exactly the two kinds of simple behavior that we have noted many times in this book.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Data Compression” (from p. 560), p. 570. Scope: lossless data compression algorithms applied to patterns from simple programs

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.86

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The named algorithm families and pattern classes are straightforward to test with public software and generated data. Full resolution is blocked by the universal claim over structurally different and future compression methods.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Generate uniform, periodic, nested, and complex patterns from known short rules, compress them with representative lossless algorithm families, and compare normalized compressed sizes. Substantial compression of complex behavior by any included general method would refute the asserted common limitation.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Essentially every method' is open-ended.

Compression ratios depend on encoding and finite sample size.

Specialized compressors can exploit known generators.

fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.72
data existence: 1.0
analysis feasibility: 0.9
operationalizability: 0.82

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The pattern classes and the compressor families are concrete, and both the generators and standard compressors are public. Compression ratios can be compared in days. The result decides the claim for the generic methods Wolfram names; it does not forbid a purpose-built encoder for one chosen rule.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Run run-length, Huffman or block, pointer-based, and two-dimensional compressors on uniform, repetitive, nested, and complex cellular-automaton patterns, including patterns from very short programs. Similar strong compression only for the first three classes confirms the claim; substantial compression of a complex short-program pattern by a generic method refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'No substantial compression' depends on length and on a numerical threshold.

A compressor designed around one particular automaton can compress that automaton; the claim is about generic methods aimed at repetition and nesting.

fields.value:

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Six structurally different lossless compression methods (run-length, block Huffman, LZ77/Deflate, LZMA, Burrows-Wheeler/bzip2 and a two-dimensional quadtree code) all strongly compress uniform and repetitive cellular automaton patterns, compress nested patterns at least partly, and achieve little compression of complex patterns from rules 30 and 45, relative to random patterns of the same density.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py generates each rule's pattern from a single black cell for 2048 steps, takes the 1024 x 1024 interior window, and compresses it with six methods: Elias-gamma run-length coding, static Huffman on 8-bit blocks (plus a 256-byte table), zlib 9, lzma 9e, bz2 9 and a quadtree code. Each size is divided by the size of a Bernoulli pattern with the same black fraction (clipped to [0.01, 0.99]) compressed by the same method, and the ratios are compared with the pre-registered class thresholds. Run time about 2 s.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Patterns: elementary CAs from a single black cell, T = 2048 steps; window rows 1024-2047, columns -512..511 (1024 x 1024 cells, inside the light cone). Classes: uniform = rule 254; repetitive = rules 50 and 250; nested = rules 90 and 150; complex = rules 30 and 45; exploratory (not in the verdict) = rule 110. Methods: (1) run-length coding of the row-major bit stream with Elias-gamma run lengths; (2) static Huffman code on non-overlapping 8-bit blocks (size = code bits + 256-byte table); (3) zlib level 9; (4) lzma preset 9 extreme; (5) bz2 level 9; (6) quadtree code of the 1024 x 1024 bitmap (1 bit 'split' or 2 bits 'uniform leaf + colour'; 1 bit per single cell). Statistic: r = size(pattern) / size(Bernoulli(d) pattern of the same shape), d = pattern's black fraction clipped to [0.01, 0.99], Bernoulli control from numpy PCG64 seed 20261031. 'supports' if all of: (a) uniform: r <= 0.10 for all 6 methods; (b) each repetitive rule: r <= 0.20 for at least 4 of 6 methods; (c) each nested rule: r <= 0.80 for at least 3 of 6 methods; (d) each complex rule: r >= 0.85 for all 6 methods.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any method achieves r < 0.60 on rule 30 or rule 45 (substantial compression of complex behavior by a generic method), or if (b) and (c) both fail (the methods do not share the ability to compress repetition and nesting). 'mixed' otherwise when any of (a)-(d) fails.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: compressed size relative to a density-matched Bernoulli pattern (r)

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: deterministic patterns; Bernoulli control sizes vary by well under 1 % between seeds (rules 50 and 250 controls: 0.00-0.03 %)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Wolfram (p. 560-570) compares run-length, block (Huffman), pointer-based (LZ) and two-dimensional schemes on CA patterns and concludes they share the same capabilities. The four families are represented by our own run-length and block-Huffman coders, three standard library compressors (zlib/Deflate and lzma are pointer-based; bzip2 adds a block-sorting family Wolfram does not discuss) and a quadtree code as the two-dimensional scheme. 'Substantial compression' is measured relative to a random pattern of the same density, so that compression explained by an unequal black/white ratio alone does not count; thresholds of 0.85 (little compression) and 0.60 (substantial) are our choice. The universal 'all methods' wording cannot be tested; a purpose-built compressor for a specific rule is outside the claim's scope (generic methods), as the assessors note.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Elementary CA rules 254, 50, 250, 90, 150, 30, 45 and 110 from a single black cell, 2048 steps; interior windows rows 1024-2047, x in [-512, 511] (generated by analysis.py)

Density-matched Bernoulli 1024 x 1024 patterns, numpy PCG64 seed 20261031 (generated by analysis.py)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Verdict 'mixed' follows the pre-registered rule because condition (a) fails on a single method: block Huffman compresses the all-black window to 16,640 bytes (12.7 % of raw, the 1-bit-per-symbol floor of a static Huffman code plus its table), which is 0.80 of what it achieves on the Bernoulli(0.99) control, not <= 0.10. This is an artefact of normalizing a uniform pattern by a nearly uniform control, a choice made at pre-registration; every other method compresses the uniform window to <= 1.1 % of the control and run-length/quadtree to essentially nothing. Under a raw-size normalization (not pre-registered) the uniform condition would hold.

The substantive claim is borne out: no method compresses rule 30 or rule 45 by more than 12 % relative to random (minimum r = 0.88, lzma on rule 30), far above the refutation threshold of 0.60, whereas every method except run-length and quadtree compresses the repetitive pattern more than 7-fold and at least four methods compress each nested pattern to <= 0.49.

The similarity of capabilities is partial, as Wolfram's own wording ('most methods') allows: run-length and quadtree coding do not compress the checkerboard (r 0.88 and 1.08) because it has no long runs or uniform blocks, and block Huffman barely compresses rule 90 (0.86).

Rules 50 and 250 produce the identical checkerboard window, so the repetitive class is effectively one pattern.

Exploratory (outside the verdict): rule 110 from a single cell, which Wolfram counts as complex, is compressed strongly by all LZ/BWT methods (r 0.06-0.11) because most of its window is the periodic background; complex patterns embedded in regular backgrounds are compressible by the generic methods.
